Example: a 405B model at 14 bytes per parameter is about 5.7 TB; at 1 TB per second of storage bandwidth that is about 6 seconds of writing.
items.used_for: Sizing storage for training clusters; asynchronous checkpointing in PyTorch Distributed Checkpoint, Orbax and NeMo. Book: Only here (Chapter 37 describes asynchronous checkpointing in words).

items.name: Owner's cost per GPU-hour, break-even rental price and cost per useful FLOP
items.formula: cost per hour of life = capital cost ÷ (useful life in years × 8,760) + power cost per hour + facility and operating cost per hour ; break-even price per sold hour = cost per hour of life ÷ utilization ; cost per useful FLOP = price per GPU-hour ÷ (peak FLOP/s × MFU × 3,600)
items.meaning: Utilization is the share of hours actually sold or used; power cost per hour = kW × price per kWh (times PUE if facility overhead is not covered elsewhere). Example from the book: a $50,000 GPU slot over 5 years ≈ $1.14 per hour, plus $0.16 of power and $0.49 of facility rent ≈ $1.79 per hour; at 70% utilization the break-even price is about $2.56 per sold hour.
items.used_for: GPU cloud pricing (CoreWeave, Lambda, hyperscalers), build-versus-rent decisions, internal chargeback. Book: Chapter 43 (Renting compute: the price of a GPU-hour; Utilization: the hotel occupancy of AI; Worked example: does a GPU pay for itself?).

items.name: Total cost of ownership (TCO) of AI infrastructure
items.formula: TCO = capital expenditure (chips, servers, network, building) + sum over years of operating expenditure (power, staff, maintenance, rent, financing) − resale value ; TCO per GPU-hour = TCO ÷ (GPUs × lifetime hours) ; building capital cost ≈ IT megawatts × cost per MW
items.meaning: The cost model of Datacenter as a Computer: capital costs are spread over each asset's life (servers about 4 to 6 years, buildings 15 to 25) and added to running costs. In AI the IT equipment usually costs several times the building per megawatt. Chip-makers and cloud providers now compete on 'tokens per dollar' or performance per TCO dollar rather than raw speed.
items.used_for: Chip purchase decisions (custom ASICs versus GPUs: Meta MTIA, Google TPU, AWS Trainium, Microsoft Maia), data-center business plans. Book: Chapter 43 (Total cost of ownership; What it costs to build: dollars per megawatt; Putting it together: a 100 MW AI data center).

items.name: Depreciation and annualized capital cost (straight-line, declining balance, capital recovery factor)
items.formula: straight-line yearly depreciation = (cost − salvage value) ÷ useful life ; declining balance: depreciation in year t = rate × book value at the start of year t ; annualized cost with financing = cost × r ÷ (1 − (1 + r)^(−n))
items.meaning: r is the yearly cost of capital and n the life in years; the last expression (the capital recovery factor) is the equal yearly payment that repays a purchase with interest, like a mortgage. Depreciation spreads a purchase over its useful life for accounting, and the assumed life of AI servers (4, 5 or 6 years) changes reported profit by billions. Example: $50,000 over 5 years: $10,000 a year straight-line; with 8% financing about $12,520 a year.
items.used_for: Hyperscaler accounting for AI servers, GPU rental pricing, TCO models. Book: Chapter 43 (Depreciation: the 4, 5 or 6-year debate).

items.name: Net present value, internal rate of return and payback
items.formula: NPV = sum over years t from 0 to n of CF_t ÷ (1 + r)^t ; IRR = the rate r at which NPV = 0 ; payback period = upfront cost ÷ yearly net cash flow (for equal yearly flows)
items.meaning: CF_t is the net cash flow in year t (negative for the purchase in year 0) and r the discount rate (cost of capital). An investment is worthwhile if NPV > 0, equivalently if its IRR beats the cost of capital. Example from the book: paying $50,000 for a GPU slot that nets $12,670 a year for 5 years: payback about 3.9 years, IRR about 8.5%; if rental prices fall 20% a year the IRR turns negative.
items.used_for: Evaluating GPU purchases, data-center projects and their financing (bonds, private credit, GPU-backed loans). Book: Chapter 43 (Worked example: does a GPU pay for itself?; Financing the buildout).

items.name: Cost per million tokens from GPU cost (and tokens per dollar)
items.formula: cost per million tokens = cost per GPU-hour ÷ (tokens per second per GPU × 3,600) × 10^6 ; tokens per dollar = tokens per second per GPU × 3,600 ÷ cost per GPU-hour ; gross margin = (price − cost) ÷ price
items.meaning: Tokens per second per GPU is total throughput across all users at the batch size actually served, which is why batching, quantization and speculative decoding cut costs; input (prefill) tokens are much cheaper to produce than output (decode) tokens. The prices customers pay, including caching discounts, are in llm-request-cost. Example: $3 per GPU-hour at 1,000 tokens per second: 3 ÷ 3,600,000 × 10^6 ≈ $0.83 per million tokens.
items.used_for: Pricing APIs; comparing serving stacks and chips on tokens per dollar. Book: Chapter 37 (From dollars per GPU-hour to dollars per million tokens), Chapter 43 (From GPU-hours to the price of a token), Chapter 33 (Worked example: how many users fit on one GPU?), Appendix B (Cost per million tokens from GPU rent).

items.name: Energy per token and per query
items.formula: joules per token = power (W) ÷ tokens per second ; facility energy per token = IT joules per token × PUE ; watt-hours per query = joules per token × tokens per query ÷ 3,600 ; tokens per second per megawatt = tokens per second per GPU × 1,000 ÷ (all-in kW per GPU × PUE)
items.meaning: Like cost per token, energy per token falls steeply with batch size because the same power serves more users. Company-reported figures: Google measured a median Gemini Apps text prompt at 0.24 Wh (August 2025, counting idle machines and data-center overhead), and OpenAI's chief executive gave about 0.34 Wh for an average ChatGPT query (June 2025); reasoning-heavy and long-context requests use many times more. Example: 1,500 W ÷ 2,000 tokens per second = 0.75 J per token; 500 tokens ≈ 375 J ≈ 0.1 Wh.
items.used_for: Energy and carbon disclosures, comparing hardware on tokens per watt, estimates of AI's energy use. Book: Appendix B (Energy per token), Chapter 44 (The energy budget), Chapter 40 (Distinction 4: per prompt versus in total).

items.name: Energy and cost of a training run
items.formula: energy (kWh) = GPUs × all-in kW per GPU × PUE × hours ; compute cost = GPU-hours × price per GPU-hour ; electricity cost = energy × price per kWh
items.meaning: Turns the training-time estimate into megawatts, megawatt-hours and dollars. Rental-equivalent cost leaves out research, failed runs, data and staff, which can exceed the final run's cost. Examples: DeepSeek-V3 reported 2.788 million H800 GPU-hours, $5.576 million at an assumed $2 per GPU-hour; Meta's model card gives about 31 million H100 GPU-hours for Llama 3.1 405B.
items.used_for: Budgeting runs, model-card energy and emissions disclosures, policy estimates of frontier training cost. Book: Chapter 37 (From days to megawatts and dollars), Chapter 19 (From FLOPs to dollars), Appendix B (GPU-hours; Rental cost of a run).

items.name: Wright's law (experience curve)
items.formula: cost of the x-th unit = C_1 × x^(−b) ; learning rate = 1 − 2^(−b) (the fractional cost drop per doubling of cumulative production)
items.meaning: C_1 is the cost of the first unit and b the experience exponent. Wright (1936) found that each doubling of cumulative aircraft production cut unit cost by a roughly fixed percentage; the same pattern describes solar panels and batteries and is used for chips and inference prices. Example: a 20% learning rate gives b = log2(1 ÷ 0.8) ≈ 0.32, so quadrupling cumulative volume cuts cost to 0.64 of its starting value.
items.used_for: Forecasting costs of solar, batteries and hardware for AI energy and compute planning. Book: Only here.

items.name: Rebound effect (Jevons paradox) condition
items.formula: total resource use = demand × resource per unit of service ; with demand ∝ price^(−ε) and price ∝ resource per unit e: total use ∝ e^(1 − ε) ; efficiency gains raise total use when ε > 1
items.meaning: ε is the price elasticity of demand. If a 10× drop in energy or cost per token brings more than a 10× rise in tokens used (ε > 1), total energy or spending rises (Jevons 1865, about coal). Whether AI demand is that elastic is a central question in forecasting AI's electricity use.
items.used_for: Forecasting data-center energy demand and compute spending as efficiency improves. Book: Chapter 37 (Efficiency and the Jevons paradox), Chapter 41 (Forecasts: why they disagree), Chapter 43.
